prompt: In the last year, when someone praised my expertise more than the situation called for, I ended up sharing more detail about my work than I meant to.
In the last year, when someone praised my expertise more than the situation called for, I kept my answer brief and did not expand on it.
In the last year, when someone stated something wrong about my work, I corrected them with the accurate details rather than letting it go.
In the last year, when someone acted skeptical or dismissive about my work, I let the comment pass without defending it in detail.
In the last year, when someone criticized my project, my team, or my employer, I responded with specific details that defended the work.
In the last year, when someone criticized my project, my team, or my employer, I held back from offering defending detail.
In the last year, when someone mentioned a modest accomplishment or figure from their own work, I shared something bigger or more specific about mine.
In the last year, even when a stranger treated me as the expert in the room, I declined to go into detail about my work.
In the last year, when someone shared something that felt confidential with me first, I offered something similarly candid about my own work in return.
In the last year, when someone offered a 'just between us' confidence, I did not match it with a candid detail about my own work.
In the last year, when a new acquaintance did me an unprompted favor, I felt I owed them something in return, including information about my work.
In the last year, when a new acquaintance did me an unprompted favor, I did not feel obligated to share work details in return.
In the last year, even with someone who was unusually attentive and easy to talk to, I kept the same limits on what I shared about my work as I would with anyone else.
In the last year, I have shared details about my work with someone I had just met because we quickly discovered a lot in common.
In the last year, noticing that someone was subtly matching my tone or body language did not make me more likely to keep talking about my work.
In the last year, when someone did something for me first, I felt obligated to return the favor, even with people I did not know well.
In the last year, when someone asked me a direct, specific question about my work, I answered it even when I was not sure I should.
In the last year, in an informal setting, I have vented about deadlines, staffing, or project setbacks to people outside my organization.
In the last year, when someone claimed not to understand my field, I explained the details of my work to them.
In the last year, I have answered detailed questions about a recent project from a recruiter or headhunter I had not verified.
In the last year, I held the same discretion about work topics in a relaxed, off-site setting that I hold in the office.
In the last year, I have skipped or declined a survey or intake form that asked about my employer, project, or role when I could not verify the sender.
In the last year, I have declined to answer questions about a colleague's or family member's work when someone asked me instead of them.
In the last year, before reviewing or commenting on technical material sent by someone I could not verify, I checked with my security office first.
In the last year, when someone spoke as though they already knew details about my work, I confirmed or filled in the gaps rather than question how they knew.
In the last year, when someone offered a rough estimate or range about my work that was off, I corrected it with the more accurate figure.
In the last year, when a question was phrased so that a plain yes or no would confirm something about my work, I answered it as asked.
In the last year, when someone cited a published detail about my organization and guessed at the rest, I confirmed or corrected their guess.
In the last year, I have discussed a hypothetical scenario related to my work without letting it lead me into specifics I would not otherwise share.
In the last year, when someone repeated a phrase I had just used back to me, I noticed it and did not feel pulled to elaborate further.
In the last year, I have noticed a conversation narrow from broad small talk down to one specific detail about my work, and redirected it.
In the last year, when someone steered talk toward a system similar to mine, I avoided drawing direct comparisons to my own work.

My public-facing profiles (professional networking sites, conference bios, social media) describe my current project or technical focus in enough detail that a stranger could tailor questions around it.
In the last year, I have discussed work specifics with a new contact I could not independently verify, at a conference, online forum, or social event.
In the last year, I have answered detailed technical questions from a stranger at a conference, trade show, or industry event.
In the last year, I have completed a survey or intake form from an organization I did not recognize that asked about my employer, project, or role.
When traveling, I treat hotel Wi-Fi, business-center computers, and hotel phone lines as though they could be monitored.
In the last year, I have posted about a current project's specifics on social media or a professional forum before it was publicly announced.
In the last year, I have challenged or reported someone without a visible badge who tried to follow me through a secure door.
Before discussing project specifics with a new professional contact, I typically verify their identity and organization through an independent channel.
